summary: Red-brick light of 1896 on the Jersey shore, its keeper's house built into the tower; lit to close the gap between Navesink and Barnegat. Now a volunteer museum.

lens.where: Sea Girt Lighthouse: a fourth-order lens bought in 2002 from Crowdy Head Lighthouse, Australia; the original was removed in 1941 or 1942

access.note: Tours on Sundays from 2 to 4 p.m. from mid-April to the Sunday before Thanksgiving, except holiday weekends; the 2026 season ran April 12 to November 22.

facts.agency: Borough of Sea Girt (owner); Sea Girt Lighthouse Citizens Committee (operator, under a lease extended to 2056)

events.note: L-shaped brick dwelling with an integral tower
Lit December 10, 1896
Fourth-order Fresnel lens, made in France
Abraham G. Wolf, first keeper
Station renamed from Squan Inlet to Sea Girt: February 1897 per the Board's report; March 1, 1897 per Sea Girt News; April 1897 per LighthouseFriends
Red flash every six seconds changed to a white flash; kerosene wick lamp replaced by an incandescent oil-vapor lamp
Storm damage noted by the Lighthouse Service Bulletin; protective works built that year
Radio beacon for fog, in commission May 1, 1921; the first land-based light so equipped
Radio beacon transmitter withdrawn and its towers dismantled
Lighthouse Service dissolved; authority passed to the Coast Guard on July 1, 1939
Light extinguished when the United States entered the Second World War; Coast Guard post with up to fifteen or twenty men
Fresnel lens removed in 1941 or 1942
Automatic light set on the tower top; no station personnel after the war
Lighthouse decommissioned
Beacon moved to a freestanding metal tower on the lawn (1954 or 1955)
Sold to the Borough of Sea Girt for $11,000 on August 10, 1956; the 22-by-24-foot metal-tower plot stayed federal
Automatic light turned off and the metal tower dismantled
25-year lease to the Sea Girt Lighthouse Citizens Committee for $1 a year; extended to 2056
Tower light installed in the lantern room; now operated as a private aid to navigation
Fourth-order lens from Crowdy Head Lighthouse, Australia, bought on eBay for $20,000 and displayed (not the original)

keepers.name: Abraham G. Wolf
keepers.note: Retired army officer, paid $1.10 a day. The committee dates his retirement to 1903. Earlier keeper of Absecon Lighthouse: 23 years per LighthouseFriends, 25 per the committee.

keepers.name: Abram L. Yates
keepers.note: Committee dates his service 1903 to 1910. Died at the lighthouse May 29, 1910, aged 58.

keepers.name: Harriet W. Yates
keepers.note: Widow of Abram Yates; acting keeper for about two months. The archive lists her under principal keepers; the committee's heading gives 1903 but its text places the service in 1910. Board refused her a permanent appointment.

keepers.name: John L. Hawkey
keepers.note: The committee prints the name as John W. Hawkey. Arrived July 23, 1910; changed the light source in 1912.

keepers.name: William H. H. Lake, Jr.
keepers.note: Born on Staten Island; the committee says he served fourteen years here and oversaw the 1921 radio beacon. Retired October 1931.

keepers.name: George J. Thomas
keepers.note: Widower; last keeper assigned by the Lighthouse Service. Last day of active duty November 29, 1940; retired March 31, 1941, pension $1,015 a year.

wrecks.outcome: Caught fire three miles offshore and was abandoned; the Citizens Committee says the station's beacon gave the crew their bearings and the lighthouse served as a first-aid station. The lighthouse's part rests on the committee's account alone.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Rowlett's directory gives 1955 and Wikidata 1977. The committee's history explains both: the Fresnel-era tower was decommissioned in 1945 with an automatic beacon on top, the beacon moved to a metal tower in 1954 or 1955, and that beacon was turned off in 1977. The record keeps 1977 as the year the light went out.

The archive roster has Wolf 1896-1902 and Abram Yates 1902-1910; the committee has Wolf to 1903 and Yates from 1903. The roster lines are kept as the archive prints them, and the committee's dates are in the notes.
The Board's report gives February 1897, Sea Girt News March 1, 1897, and LighthouseFriends April 1897. The story gives the Board's month, the primary record.
The archive gives 52 feet above mean high water (about 16 m); Sea Girt News gives the lamp at 60 feet (18 m), and Wikipedia repeats 60 feet. The record keeps 18 m, pending a Light List check.

notes_for_editor: Keeper dates conflict across the archive roster, LighthouseFriends and the Citizens Committee (Wolf to 1902 or 1903; Abram Yates from 1902 or 1903; Hawkey John L. or John W.). The committee's keepers page heads Harriet Yates's acting term 'May 29-July 23, 1903' but its text places it in 1910, which the archive roster supports. The Wolf Civil War story rests only on the committee and LighthouseFriends; no contemporary record was found, and the story says so. The Morro Castle claims about the beacon and the first-aid station come only from the committee's home page; a Chronicling America search for Morro Castle and Sea Girt returned many pages and none was read, so this is unverified. The keeper's son is unnamed, and the Coast Guard seaman on the last post is unnamed, under the living-person rule. The USLHS place record puts the station at 41.63 N, 74.02 W, about 1.5 degrees of latitude north of the real site; our record's OSM position (40.1366, -74.0275) matches LighthouseFriends and Sea Girt News, so no correction is proposed to our location. The record's tower height is 13.4 m, the 44 feet the committee gives (fact-check 2026-10-28). LighthouseFriends is copyrighted: facts only, in our own words. The 1887 Board report is quoted through LighthouseFriends; the corpus Board volumes start in 1891. The 1921 radio service and the 1915 storm damage are in Board, Commissioner and Bulletin sources; the Commissioner page cited is a bound volume (1915-1922), not the 1921 report alone.
